# Slack vs Element (2026)

## Overview
Slack and Element are team communication platforms designed to facilitate collaboration and information sharing among team members. This comparison is beneficial for teams considering switching from Slack to Element, particularly those prioritizing data ownership and customizability. The core use case for both tools is team communication, and the key reason someone would switch is to gain more control over their data and reduce costs.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Element is free and self-hosted, while Slack charges per user.
* Data ownership: Element allows teams to host their data on their own servers, while Slack stores data on its servers.
* Setup complexity: Element requires more technical expertise to set up and maintain, while Slack is generally easier to set up.
* Scalability: Element can be more scalable than Slack, especially for large teams, since it can be self-hosted.
* Feature difference: Element has end-to-end encryption for all conversations, while Slack only offers this feature for paid plans.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Slack | Element |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $7.25-$15/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | Apache 2.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $362.50-$750/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1,450-$3,000/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
### Slack
* Easy to set up and use
* Wide range of integrations with third-party apps
* Good mobile app support
* Large user community
* Limited control over data storage and security
### Element
* Self-hosting option for data control and security
* End-to-end encryption for all conversations
* Customizable and extensible
* Free and open-source
* Steeper learning curve and more technical expertise required

## When to Choose Each
Slack is a good choice for teams that prioritize ease of use and a wide range of integrations with third-party apps. It's suitable for small to medium-sized teams that don't require a high level of customizability and are willing to pay for a proprietary solution. Element, on the other hand, is a good choice for teams that require a high level of control over their data and security. It's suitable for larger teams or organizations that need to comply with strict data regulations and are willing to invest in self-hosting and customization.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Slack data using the Slack export tool, which provides a JSON file containing your team's messages, files, and other data.
2. Set up an Element server and configure it according to your team's needs.
3. Use the Element import tool to import your Slack data into Element.
4. Configure any necessary integrations and settings in Element.

---

## Our Take
Element is not yet production-ready for most users due to its limited user interface and lack of polish compared to Slack. One specific technical limitation worth knowing before switching is that Element's search functionality is not as robust as Slack's. However, for teams that require a high level of control over their data and security, Element is a good choice, and we recommend switching to Element if you're a large team or organization with strict data regulations.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams (less than 10 users) that don't need a wide range of integrations and want to save on costs
* Large teams (more than 50 users) that require a high level of control over their data and security
* Organizations with strict data regulations that need to comply with GDPR or HIPAA
* Teams that don't need advanced features like screen sharing and video conferencing
* Developers who want a customizable and extensible team communication platform

## FAQ
### Can I use Element for free?
Yes, Element is free and open-source, and you can self-host it on your own server.
### Is Element as easy to use as Slack?
No, Element has a steeper learning curve and requires more technical expertise to set up and use.
### Can I integrate Element with third-party apps?
Yes, Element has a wide range of integrations with third-party apps, although not as many as Slack.
### Is Element secure?
Yes, Element offers end-to-end encryption for all conversations and allows teams to host their data on their own servers.
### Can I migrate my Slack data to Element?
Yes, you can export your Slack data and import it into Element using the Element import tool.

# Slack vs Mattermost (2026)

## Overview
Slack and Mattermost are two popular communication platforms designed for teams and organizations. This comparison is beneficial for those looking to switch from Slack to Mattermost, particularly for teams prioritizing data ownership and customization. The core use case for both tools is team collaboration, and the key reason someone would switch is to gain more control over their data and reduce costs.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Slack charges per user, while Mattermost offers a free, self-hosted option.
* Data ownership: Mattermost allows teams to host their own servers, giving them full control over their data, whereas Slack stores data on its own servers.
* Setup complexity: Slack is generally easier to set up, with a more streamlined onboarding process, while Mattermost requires more technical expertise to self-host.
* Scalability: Mattermost is designed to scale horizontally, making it more suitable for large, distributed teams, while Slack's scalability is more dependent on its proprietary infrastructure.
* Integration with GitHub: Mattermost has native integration with GitHub, allowing for seamless issue tracking and project management, whereas Slack relies on third-party integrations.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Slack | Mattermost |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $7.25-$15/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | MIT / AGPL |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $362.50-$750/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1450-$3000/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
### Slack
* Easy to set up and use
* Wide range of integrations with third-party tools
* Robust mobile apps
* Strong customer support
* Limited control over data ownership and storage
### Mattermost
* Self-hosted option for full data control
* Customizable and extensible through plugins and APIs
* Scalable and performant for large teams
* Free, open-source option
* Steeper learning curve due to self-hosting requirements
* Limited support for certain integrations and plugins

## When to Choose Each
Slack is suitable for small to medium-sized teams that prioritize ease of use and a wide range of integrations. It's ideal for teams that don't require full control over their data and are willing to pay a premium for convenience. On the other hand, Mattermost is designed for larger teams or organizations that require customization, scalability, and data ownership. It's perfect for teams with technical expertise and a desire for self-hosting, as well as those looking to reduce costs and increase control over their communication platform.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Slack data using the Slack API or a third-party tool, such as the Slack Exporter.
2. Set up a Mattermost server, either self-hosted or through a cloud provider.
3. Import your Slack data into Mattermost using the Mattermost API or a compatible import tool.
4. Configure your Mattermost instance, including setting up users, channels, and plugins.
5. Test your Mattermost instance to ensure a smooth transition from Slack.

## Our Take
Mattermost is a production-ready alternative to Slack for most users, offering a robust and customizable communication platform. However, one specific technical limitation worth knowing is that Mattermost's self-hosted option requires significant technical expertise, which may be a barrier for smaller teams or those without dedicated IT support. Based on our analysis, we recommend switching to Mattermost for teams that prioritize data ownership, customization, and cost-effectiveness, while smaller teams or those requiring a more streamlined onboarding process may be better off with Slack.

## Who Should Switch
* Large teams (100+ users) looking to reduce costs and increase control over their data
* Technical teams that require customization and extensibility through plugins and APIs
* Organizations prioritizing data ownership and security
* Teams with existing self-hosted infrastructure looking to integrate a communication platform
* Open-source enthusiasts who value the freedom to modify and extend their software

## FAQ
### Is Mattermost free?
Mattermost offers a free, self-hosted option, as well as a range of paid plans with additional features and support.
### Can I self-host Slack?
No, Slack does not offer a self-hosted option.
### Is Mattermost compatible with Slack integrations?
Mattermost has a range of integrations with popular tools, but may not be compatible with all Slack integrations.
### How long does it take to set up Mattermost?
The setup time for Mattermost varies depending on the complexity of your instance and the level of technical expertise, but can range from a few hours to several days.
### Can I migrate my Slack data to Mattermost?
Yes, you can export your Slack data and import it into Mattermost using the Mattermost API or a compatible import tool.

title: Notion vs Obsidian

# Notion vs Obsidian

## Overview

All-in-one workspace combining notes, databases, wikis, and project management. is a popular proprietary tool in the productivity space. Obsidian is a free, open-source alternative that gives organizations complete control over their data and deployment.

## Key Differences

- **Cost**: Notion costs $8-$20/user/month; Obsidian is Free (local use)
- **License**: Notion is Proprietary; Obsidian is Proprietary (free personal)
- **Data ownership**: Obsidian can be self-hosted so your data stays on infrastructure you control
- **Vendor lock-in**: Obsidian eliminates dependency on a single commercial vendor
- **Community**: Obsidian has an active open-source community contributing features and fixes

## Pricing Comparison

| Aspect | Notion | Obsidian |
|--------|-------------------------------|-------------------------------|
| Base pricing | $8-$20/user/month | Free (local use) |
| License | Proprietary | Proprietary (free personal) |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Cost at 50 users | ~$400/month | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Cost at 200 users | ~$1,600/month | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Vendor lock-in | High | None |

## Pros and Cons

### Notion

**Pros:**
- Polished, professionally designed user interface
- Large ecosystem of official integrations
- Managed infrastructure with no server maintenance required
- Enterprise SLA and dedicated support available
- Mobile apps are well-maintained and reliable

**Cons:**
- Significant per-user monthly cost that scales linearly with team size
- Your data is stored on the vendor infrastructure
- No ability to inspect or modify the source code
- Feature roadmap controlled entirely by the vendor
- Risk of pricing changes, acquisition, or discontinuation

### Obsidian

**Pros:**
- Free to self-host with costs only for server infrastructure
- Complete data ownership and privacy control
- Source code is auditable and modifiable
- Active open-source community
- No vendor lock-in or risk of sudden pricing changes

**Cons:**
- Requires technical knowledge to self-host and maintain
- May lack some advanced features found in the proprietary version
- Support relies on community forums rather than a paid helpdesk
- UI polish may lag behind the proprietary tool
- You are responsible for updates, backups, and security patches

## When to Choose Each

**Choose Notion if:** Notion is the right choice when you need the most polished user experience, the broadest integration ecosystem, and professional support with SLA guarantees.

**Choose Obsidian if:** Obsidian is ideal for privacy-conscious teams, organizations with strict data sovereignty requirements, or anyone wanting to eliminate per-seat subscription costs.

## Migration Path

Export your data from Notion in its standard export format, review Obsidian import documentation, and plan a pilot period where both tools run in parallel.

## Our Take

Obsidian is production-ready for most teams willing to invest a few hours in setup. The self-hosted version gives you identical or better functionality to the paid Notion tiers, with no recurring per-seat cost.

The main technical limitation worth knowing: you are responsible for your own backups, updates, and uptime. If your server goes down, so does your Obsidian instance. Plan for this with automated backups and a monitoring alert.

Our recommendation: if your team has at least one developer and you are paying more than $100/month for Notion, switching to self-hosted Obsidian will pay for itself within the first month. If nobody on your team is comfortable with Linux or Docker, stay on Notion until you have that resource.

## Who Should Switch

- Startups under 20 people paying per-seat fees they cannot yet justify
- Dev teams who already self-host other tools and have the ops knowledge
- Organizations in jurisdictions with strict data residency requirements
- Teams who have evaluated Notion paid features and only use the basics
- Founders and solopreneurs who want the functionality without the subscription

## FAQ

### Is Obsidian free to use?
Yes. Obsidian is free to self-host. Your only cost is the server, typically $6-$12/month on a VPS provider like DigitalOcean or Vultr.

### How hard is it to migrate from Notion to Obsidian?
For most teams, migration takes 2-4 hours. Export your Notion data, follow the Obsidian import guide, and test with a small group before switching everyone over.

### Does Obsidian get regular updates?
Yes. Obsidian has an active open-source community with regular releases. Check the GitHub repository for release frequency.

### Can I use Obsidian without technical knowledge?
You need basic comfort with a VPS and command line. If that feels unfamiliar, there are managed hosting options that handle the server for you at a modest cost.

### What happens if Obsidian development stops?
Because the source code is open, you can continue running whatever version you have indefinitely. You can also fork the project or switch to another tool at your own pace — no vendor can shut off your instance.

---
*Data sourced June 2026. Pricing and features change. Verify at [Notion](https://notion.so) and [Obsidian](https://obsidian.md) before making decisions.*

title: GitHub vs GitLab
comparison_markdown:
# GitHub vs GitLab

## Overview

GitHub is the world largest code hosting platform, owned by Microsoft, with 100 million developers. GitLab is a complete DevOps platform that can be fully self-hosted, offering everything from Git hosting to CI/CD and container registries.

## Key Differences

- **Cost**: GitHub free tier is generous; GitLab Community Edition is fully free to self-host
- **CI/CD**: GitLab has more powerful built-in CI/CD pipelines; GitHub Actions is catching up
- **Self-hosting**: GitLab is designed to be self-hosted; GitHub Enterprise self-hosted is expensive
- **Feature scope**: GitLab is a complete DevSecOps platform; GitHub focuses on developer collaboration
- **Community**: GitHub has a dramatically larger open-source community and project discoverability

## Pricing Comparison

| Aspect | GitHub | GitLab |
|--------|-------------------------------|-------------------------------|
| Base pricing | Free / $7-$21/user | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | MIT (CE) |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Cost at 50 users | See pricing page | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Cost at 200 users | See pricing page | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Vendor lock-in | High | None |

## Pros and Cons

### GitHub

**Pros:**
- Polished, professionally designed user interface
- Large ecosystem of official integrations
- Managed infrastructure with no server maintenance required
- Enterprise SLA and dedicated support available
- Mobile apps are well-maintained and reliable

**Cons:**
- Significant per-user monthly cost that scales linearly with team size
- Your data is stored on the vendor infrastructure
- No ability to inspect or modify the source code
- Feature roadmap controlled entirely by the vendor
- Risk of pricing changes, acquisition, or discontinuation

### GitLab

**Pros:**
- Free to self-host with costs only for server infrastructure
- Complete data ownership and privacy control
- Source code is auditable and modifiable
- Active open-source community
- No vendor lock-in or risk of sudden pricing changes
> GitHub: [gitlabhq/gitlabhq](https://github.com/gitlabhq/gitlabhq) * ~24k stars

**Cons:**
- Requires technical knowledge to self-host and maintain
- May lack some advanced features found in the proprietary version
- Support relies on community forums rather than a paid helpdesk
- UI polish may lag behind the proprietary tool
- You are responsible for updates, backups, and security patches

## When to Choose Each

**Choose GitHub if:** GitHub suits open-source projects wanting maximum community visibility or teams deeply integrated with GitHub Actions workflows.

**Choose GitLab if:** GitLab self-hosted is ideal for enterprises needing full control over their DevOps stack or regulated industries.

## Migration Path

GitLab provides a GitHub importer that migrates repositories, issues, PRs, wikis, and milestones. Update CI configuration from GitHub Actions to GitLab CI/CD YAML format.

## Our Take

GitLab is production-ready for most teams willing to invest a few hours in setup. The self-hosted version gives you identical or better functionality to the paid GitHub tiers, with no recurring per-seat cost.

The main technical limitation worth knowing: you are responsible for your own backups, updates, and uptime. If your server goes down, so does your GitLab instance. Plan for this with automated backups and a monitoring alert.

Our recommendation: if your team has at least one developer and you are paying more than $100/month for GitHub, switching to self-hosted GitLab will pay for itself within the first month. If nobody on your team is comfortable with Linux or Docker, stay on GitHub until you have that resource.

## Who Should Switch

- Startups under 20 people paying per-seat fees they cannot yet justify
- Dev teams who already self-host other tools and have the ops knowledge
- Organizations in jurisdictions with strict data residency requirements
- Teams who have evaluated GitHub paid features and only use the basics
- Founders and solopreneurs who want the functionality without the subscription

## FAQ

### Is GitLab free to use?
Yes. GitLab is free to self-host. Your only cost is the server, typically $6-$12/month on a VPS provider like DigitalOcean or Vultr.

### How hard is it to migrate from GitHub to GitLab?
For most teams, migration takes 2-4 hours. Export your GitHub data, follow the GitLab import guide, and test with a small group before switching everyone over.

### Does GitLab get regular updates?
Yes. GitLab has an active open-source community with regular releases. Check the GitHub repository for release frequency.

### Can I use GitLab without technical knowledge?
You need basic comfort with a VPS and command line. If that feels unfamiliar, there are managed hosting options that handle the server for you at a modest cost.

### What happens if GitLab development stops?
Because the source code is open, you can continue running whatever version you have indefinitely. You can also fork the project or switch to another tool at your own pace — no vendor can shut off your instance.

---
*Data sourced June 2026. Pricing and features change. Verify at [GitHub](https://github.com) and [GitLab](https://gitlab.com) before making decisions.*
meta_description: GitLab is a free, self-hosted alternative to GitHub. Compare pricing, features, and migration steps. See full comparison.

title: Figma vs Penpot
comparison_markdown:
# Figma vs Penpot (2026)

## Overview
Figma and Penpot are two popular design and prototyping tools used by designers, developers, and product teams to create user interfaces, wireframes, and high-fidelity prototypes. This comparison is beneficial for teams and individuals who are looking for a cost-effective and scalable design solution, with the core use case being collaborative design and prototyping. The key reason someone would switch from Figma to Penpot is to take advantage of Penpot's free and open-source nature, as well as its self-hosting capabilities.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Figma offers a free plan with limited features, while Penpot is completely free and open-source.
* Data ownership: Penpot allows users to self-host and have full control over their data, while Figma stores data on its proprietary servers.
* Setup complexity: Figma has a more straightforward setup process, while Penpot requires more technical expertise to self-host.
* Scalability: Penpot is highly scalable due to its open-source nature and self-hosting capabilities, while Figma's scalability is limited by its proprietary architecture.
* Integration with GitHub: Penpot has native integration with GitHub, allowing for seamless version control and collaboration, while Figma relies on third-party integrations.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Figma | Penpot |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $12-$75/user/month | Free |
| License | Proprietary | MPL 2.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $600-$3750/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $2400-$15,000/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
**Figma:**
* Pros:
	+ Easy to use and intuitive interface
	+ Large community and plenty of resources
	+ Seamless collaboration and real-time feedback
	+ Wide range of integrations with other design tools
	+ Robust customer support
* Cons:
	+ Expensive, especially for large teams
	+ Limited control over data and security
	+ Proprietary architecture can limit scalability
	+ Limited customization options
	+ Can be slow and buggy at times
**Penpot:**
* Pros:
	+ Completely free and open-source
	+ Self-hosting capabilities for full control over data
	+ Highly scalable and customizable
	+ Native integration with GitHub
	+ Active community and growing ecosystem
* Cons:
	+ Steeper learning curve due to technical requirements
	+ Limited resources and community compared to Figma
	+ Some features still in development or missing
	+ Can be overwhelming for small teams or individuals
	+ Limited customer support

## When to Choose Each
Figma is a good choice for teams who prioritize ease of use, a large community, and seamless collaboration, and are willing to pay a premium for these features. This includes large design teams, enterprises, and agencies who require robust customer support and a wide range of integrations. On the other hand, Penpot is a good choice for teams who value flexibility, scalability, and control over their data, and are willing to invest time and resources into self-hosting and customization. This includes open-source enthusiasts, small to medium-sized teams, and individuals who are looking for a cost-effective and customizable design solution.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Figma designs in SVG or PNG format.
2. Use the Penpot import tool to import your designs into Penpot.
3. Configure your Penpot instance to match your Figma workflow, including setting up users, teams, and permissions.
4. Update your design files to take advantage of Penpot's features and capabilities.
5. Test and refine your Penpot setup to ensure a smooth transition.

## Our Take
Penpot is not yet production-ready for most users, as it still lacks some key features and has a limited community compared to Figma. One specific technical limitation worth knowing is that Penpot's self-hosting capabilities require a significant amount of technical expertise, which can be a barrier for small teams or individuals. However, for teams who value flexibility, scalability, and control over their data, Penpot is a clear winner, and we recommend switching from Figma to take advantage of its free and open-source nature.

## Who Should Switch
* Small to medium-sized design teams who don't need advanced features like augmented reality or 3D modeling
* Open-source enthusiasts who value customization and control over their data
* Individuals who are looking for a cost-effective and scalable design solution
* Teams who prioritize data security and self-hosting capabilities
* Developers who want to integrate design tools with their existing GitHub workflow

## FAQ
### Can I use Penpot for free?
Yes, Penpot is completely free and open-source, with no costs or limitations on usage.
### Is Penpot compatible with Figma files?
Yes, Penpot can import Figma designs in SVG or PNG format, and also supports Figma's API for seamless integration.
### Does Penpot have a mobile app?
Not yet, but Penpot has a responsive web interface that can be accessed on mobile devices.
### Can I self-host Penpot on my own server?
Yes, Penpot allows self-hosting on your own server, giving you full control over your data and security.
### Is Penpot suitable for large enterprises?
Not yet, as Penpot still lacks some key features and has a limited community compared to Figma, but it is a good choice for small to medium-sized teams and individuals.
